overview: ‘Audiovisuel public : Les secrets d'une commission d'enquête’ takes us behind the scenes of the highly publicised parliamentary committee of inquiry into public broadcasting.  Chaired by Horizons MP Jérémie Patrier-Leitus, with Charles Alloncle – MP and spokesperson for the Union of the Right for the Republic – acting as rapporteur, this committee has shed unprecedented light on the work of parliamentarians, at times in a controversial manner.  This previously unseen documentary details the legislative process, which is little known to the general public. Throughout the film, the MPs on the committee share their exclusive accounts of the origins of an inquiry committee, the practical role of the parliamentarians who sit on it, the mechanics of the hearings and, implicitly, a fundamental questioning of the real usefulness of such committees.

original_title: Contracts of making viewing and listening
overview: Contracts of making, viewing, and listening is an artistic intervention into Satyajit Ray’s Ashani Sanket (Distant Thunder), made in 1973; the film tells the story of the effects of famine in rural Bengal through the eyes of a Brahmin couple. In Ray’s Ashani Sanket, the only Dalit woman the audience meets is Moti, who appears in brief spurts to highlight the humanity of the Brahmin protagonists and to testify to the restrictions of caste that these protagonists are meant to transgress by way of consummating their humanity. Moti is accorded only a fraction of the film's screen time and spoken parts, and is promptly relegated to the background once her narrative purpose is met.  The artistic intervention is geared towards critically reading the film through the lens of Dalit consciousness, and exploring ways of writing that critique in and through the language of the film itself.

title: Salvaje
overview: "Savage" is a term with clear derogatory connotations. While it designates what is external to human society, the same concept also encompasses other cultures, viewed as inferior. It stems from a delusion of grandeur born of an inability to understand logic different from one's own. For a long time, the West labeled the indigenous societies of the Americas as "savages" and "barbaric," investing considerable effort in the "civilizing work."

In the Lucre Valley, Cusco, Peru, the Wool Spinning and Weaving Factory was founded in 1861, considered the first modern textile industry in Peru and South America. The factory was the only one to continue the textile activity that the Obraje Hacienda Nuestra Señora de la Asunción had been carrying out since 1715. Studded in history and tradition, over the years it achieved a high-quality textile production, recognized worldwide. Peru's historical context meant that the factory supplied clothing to royalist, revolutionary, and republican armies, and even to foreign armies due to the export of textiles to the Philippines, the United States, and Spain during the World Wars. Production at the Lucre factory declined around 1968, when it was expropriated, entering a period of debt and conflict that resulted in its eventual bankruptcy. Currently, the factory is undergoing a slow process of restoration and revitalization, with the aim of becoming a tourist attraction.

original_title: Karen Williams: I Had To Laugh
overview: Karen Williams burst onto the San Francisco Bay Area comedy circuit in the early 1980s. As the country’s first openly lesbian Black comic to use specifically lesbian material, Karen’s humor was unlike any other. A feminist and LGBTQ+ rights activist, Williams became known for her quick repartee and insightful commentary. But while her popularity as a performer grew, off-stage she was a single mom, struggling to raise her children. In 1988, Karen founded the HaHa Institute, dedicated to helping others find healing through humor. Award-winning director Andrea Meyerson brings Karen Williams' story to the screen, covering her hard-fought battle to break into male-dominated comedy clubs and the joy that has guided her through it all. Rarely-seen vintage performance footage woven together with interviews from family members and industry colleagues—including Kate Clinton, Marga Gomez, and Diane Amos, as well as Karen herself—reveal the life of this amazingly creative and prolific woman.
